title: GPU Reserve Curve Simulator & Procurement Notes — Private VPC
body:
Purpose:
Provide a compact simulator-style workbook and procurement notes for Private/VPC GPU fleets. Focus is on a reserve-curve (percentile-based headroom) approach that maps seasonality and burst buffers to discrete purchase tranches and SKU mixes. This is an early working model: rough CAPEX/OPEX, tranche timing, and region split recommendations for 12–36 month procurement planning.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Use a reserve-curve target of p95 latency/throughput headroom to size baseline fleet; map p99 surge to burst/partner-cloud.
- Prefer heterogeneous mixes (H100-heavy for high-QPS Q4 routes, A100 / L4 for mid/low cost) with 20–30% spare capacity cushion.
- Stagger hardware purchases in 3 tranches over 18 months to capture price drops and reduce idle cost.

Key assumptions (editable inputs):
- Baseline 12-month avg QPS growth: 3.5% month-over-month (configurable)
- Current running model mix: 40% H100 (high perf), 40% A100, 20% L4 (cost-optimized).
- Effective concurrent sessions per GPU (avg util): H100=60, A100=45, L4=28 (tokens/sec proxy).
- Target utilization band for steady-state: 70–80% (target=75%).
- Reserve curve percentiles: steady (p50), headroom (p95), surge (p99).
- Planning horizon: 36 months. Discount factor for deferred purchases: 2% per quarter.

Inputs table (example):
region,initial-qps,monthly-growth,latency-slo-ms,target-reserve-pct
us-west,125000,0.035,150,0.20
us-east,210000,0.032,120,0.25
eu-central,90000,0.030,160,0.20

Workings (how the simulator maps inputs to hardware):
1) Convert QPS -> token/sec throughput estimate (tokens per request default 220).
2) Map token/sec to GPU slots via per-SKU effective throughput (see assumptions).
3) Apply target utilization to compute raw required GPUs.
4) Add reserve (p95 headroom) as percent of raw required to get baseline capacity.
5) Map baseline capacity to discrete chassis purchases (e.g., 8x A100 per rack) with spare-drive accounting.
6) For p99 surge, evaluate partner-cloud overflow and hot-swap failover budget (soft capacity).

Sample calculation snippet (us-west, month 0):
- QPS=125k req/s * 220 tokens = 27.5M tokens/s total
- Effective tokens/s per GPU (H100)=60 * 1k = 60k tokens/s (note: units are a simplification for sheet)
- Equivalent H100 GPUs needed (no reserve) = 27.5M / 60k = ~458 GPUs
- Apply target utilization (75%) -> 458 / 0.75 = 611 GPUs baseline
- Add reserve p95 (20%) = 611 * 1.20 = 733 GPUs baseline rounded -> discretize by node size (e.g., 8-GPU node -> 92 nodes)

Procurement tranche model (recommended):
- Tranche A (Q1): purchase 40% of baseline, target immediate need + minimal cushion. Prioritize a mix biased to A100+L4 to reduce near-term spend.
- Tranche B (Q3): purchase additional 35% after monitoring adoption. Shift mix toward more H100 if latency-sensitive features have traction.
- Tranche C (Q5): final 25% to fill to peak baseline and add 10% spare for next-year runway. Reserve option/PO for additional units if price drops >10%.

Cost model sketch (placeholders — update with vendor quotes):
- Unit list price (example): H100 GPU node (8x) = $420k; A100 node (8x) = $280k; L4 node (8x) = $95k.
- Annual maintenance / support: 10% list. Power and rack OPEX: $12k per rack/year (depends on data center).
- Example: us-west tranche A (92 nodes A100 mix -> 40% of baseline) -> CAPEX estimate = $X (sheet computes per mix).

Discretization rules (important to avoid weird partial-node buys):
- Minimum buy unit = 1 node (8 GPU typical).
- Allow reserved PO options for convertible units (e.g., buy chassis, swap GPUs later).
- Overprovision rounding: round up to nearest whole node; prefer odd-even rack balancing across AZs.

Region split and latency considerations:
- Map baseline capacity to regions by traffic origin percentile. If p95 headroom in one region exceeds 40% of baseline, evaluate spillover lanes to neighboring region and increase inter-region replication.
- For regulated customers requiring data residency, allocate dedicated fraction of baseline (config) and tag as "pinned capacity" in BOM.

Example output table (collapsed):
region,baseline-gpus,baseline-nodes,trancheA-nodes,trancheB-nodes,trancheC-nodes,total-capex-approx
us-west,733,92,37,32,23,$10.9M
us-east,1240,155,62,54,39,$18.3M
eu-central,528,66,26,23,17,$6.1M

Recommendations and levers to tune:
- Move low-latency load to H100 only when p95 latency violations >1% over a week.
- Use spot / partner-cloud for predictable p99 bursts instead of buying full p99 capacity.
- Maintain a 3–4 month spare parts pool (spare GPUs and spare chassis) to avoid procurement lag risk.
- Negotiate price-protection clauses for tranche B/C to capture vendor price drops.

Open questions & TODOs:
- Get updated vendor quotes and preferred SKU list by region (Asha to own).
- Confirm exact tokens-per-request distribution by product route (Product data team).
- Validate per-SKU throughput numbers with Applied ML bench harness (Lina/Carlos).
- Add a column for quantized runtime variants (e.g., 4-bit profiles) and their throughput multipliers.

Appendix: quick sensitivity checks to run in the sheet (recommended pivots)
- Vary reserve curve between 10% and 40% and observe idle cost delta.
- Shift SKU mix by ±10% H100 and see latency vs. CAPEX tradeoff.
- Run 3 purchase timing variants (front-loaded, evenly spaced, back-loaded) and compare NPV of CAPEX + expected idle OPEX.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working simulator; the numbers above are illustrative. Please update vendor pricing and real throughput benchmarks.
- I intentionally kept the model coarse-grained so we can iterate quickly; follow-up will convert to a linked sheet with automated vendor pricing inputs and a simple dashboard.

Last edits: 2026-01-12 — moved tranche timing forward after procurement call, added p95/p99 language and partner-cloud overflow notes.
